title: Quandaries & Quagmires: Risky business: Professional liability claims
author: Jennifer Bovitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not address legal AI, jagged task capability, selective deployment, verification of AI output, or AI-driven workflow redesign. Its recommendations on supervision and documentation are broadly compatible with the cluster’s governance emphasis, but they concern general professional-liability controls and do not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: Implement supervisory procedures and training for associates and staff.
File maintenance and documentation are imperative, including documenting critical client advice.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: Bovitz supports the synthesis’s central distinction between emerging insurer concern about AI and evidence of actual AI-related malpractice incidence. She places AI within broader, established loss drivers, rising defense costs and catastrophic claims linked chiefly to problematic clients, while emphasizing that differing study populations limit comparisons.

kp.k: Insurers identify AI among major liability concerns
kp.d: Bovitz reports that the EPIC Study identified attorney supervision, cyber, and AI risk as top concerns for insurers of AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 firms. This is a reported insurer concern, not a quantified finding of AI-caused malpractice or a prediction of workforce restructuring.
qs: The EPIC Study found that insurers noted attorney supervision, cyber, and AI risk as top areas of concern for their AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 insured firms.

kp.k: Studies cover different populations and liability outcomes
kp.d: The article synthesizes the ABA's 2020-2023 insurer-supplied malpractice data, an EPIC survey of 11 insurers collectively covering more than 80% of AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 firms, anonymously reported information from two large- and midsize-firm insurers in the Lockton Report, and Minnesota disciplinary reporting. Bovitz cautions that big law is generally absent from the ABA sample.
qs: An important limitation to the study is that big law is generally not represented.

A separate study conducted by Eileen Garczynski at [EPIC Law Firm Group](https://minnlawyer.com/tag/epic-law-firm-group/?taxo-tag-body) polled 11 professional liability insurers that combined provide coverage to more than 80% of AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 firms
Additionally, Doug Richmond and Andrew Ricke recently compiled information from two leading insurers of large and midsize firms and reported the data anonymously

kp.k: Estates and transactional work feature prominently in claims
kp.d: In the ABA Study, estate, trust, and probate rose from fourth to first in claim frequency, followed by real estate and plaintiff personal injury; the article attributes the estates shift to population aging and wealth transfer. EPIC also placed trusts and estates among its top three claim-generating areas. Lockton found transactional practices generated claims most frequently, offering easier proof of negligence, greater potential compensatory damages, and growing third-party claims as explanations rather than demonstrated causal findings.
qs: For context, estate, trust, and probate increased in risk from its previous fourth-place ranking to now atop the leaderboard.
This shift in frequency is attributed to the aging population and the highest transfer of wealth comparatively to any other time in the United States.

In the Lockton Report, a notable finding was that although the insurers surveyed covered firms who had both litigation and transactional practices, the transactional practices were the most frequent source of claims.

kp.k: Most claims yield no payment; defense costs increase
kp.d: Bovitz reports that 82% of claims in the ABA Study resulted in no claim payment and that indemnity-payment severity declined when payments occurred. Separately, 10 of EPIC's 11 insurers reported increased defense costs. She emphasizes that absence of indemnity does not remove the stress of claims for lawyers and firms.
qs: Eighty-two percent of claims in the ABA Study resulted in no payment of the claim and a decrease in severity of indemnity payments when claims were paid.
The EPIC study also reported on the increasing cost to defend professional liability claims, with 10 out of the 11 insurers reporting increases in defense costs.

kp.k: Small firms dominate claims; larger-firm shares increase
kp.d: The ABA Study found that firms with five or fewer attorneys accounted for most claims but also experienced the largest net decrease, alongside increases for every other firm-size group. The article reports that firms with more than 500 lawyers accounted for 11.10% of claims in 2023, versus 4.62% in the 2019 study, describing the change as a 6.48% increase. These findings retain the article's qualification about limited big-law representation.
qs: The ABA study concluded that firms with five or less attorneys comprised most claims.
Firms with more than 500 lawyers saw a 6.48% increase in claims for a total of 11.10% of all claims in 2023 compared to 4.62% in the 2019 study.

kp.k: Substantive and administrative errors drive routine liability
kp.d: The article identifies document preparation and filing, commencement of proceedings, advice, pretrial work, and settlement negotiation as the consistently leading claim-generating activities. Substantive errors are the largest alleged error category, followed by administrative errors and client-relations errors; intentional wrongs are least frequent. Reported increases include untimely commencement of actions at 2.73%, drafting errors at 3.99%, and conflicts at 2.89%.
qs: Substantive errors are the largest error category alleged in claims and include failing to know and/or apply the law, drafting errors, conflicts, inadequate discovery/investigation, failure to know/ascertain a deadline, failure to understand/anticipate tax, errors in public record search, and errors in mathematical calculation.

Lawyers are much more likely to experience a claim because they failed to commence an action in a timely matter (up 2.73%), had a drafting error (up 3.99%) or engaged in a conflict of interest (up 2.89%).

kp.k: Catastrophic claims frequently involve dishonest clients
kp.d: Lockton identified 83 publicly reported law-firm settlements or verdicts exceeding $20 million dating to the mid-1980s; the largest was $390 million in 2020, the average $47.4 million, and the median $34.5 million. Bovitz reports that representation of 'unworthy' clients accounted for two-thirds of catastrophic payments, with conflicts next most prominent. Transactional or corporate work accounted for 29 cases and securities for 17. The article argues that such clients target larger firms for reputational benefits and that harmed third parties often pursue the claims.
qs: The Lockton Report identified 83 publicly reported settlements or verdicts exceeding $20 million involving law firms dating back to the mid-1980s, with the largest being a $390 million settlement in 2020.
The average settlement or verdict was $47.4 million, with the median at $34.5 million.

Representation of an unworthy client represents two-thirds of the reported catastrophic payments, and 17 of the cases in this category involved firms of 1,501 lawyers or more and 26 involved firms with 251-500 lawyers.
Unworthy clients often target larger law firms to benefit from perceived or actual reputational factors.

kp.k: Disciplinary reporting highlights communication and client-property failures
kp.d: Minnesota recorded 27 publicly disciplined and 101 privately disciplined lawyers in 2024. Public outcomes comprised five disbarments, 14 suspensions, and eight reprimands, with two reprimanded lawyers also placed on probation. Private discipline included 95 admonitions involving 243 Rule violations and six probation agreements. Communication and safekeeping-property violations led admonitions. Bovitz treats disciplinary complaints as a potential precursor to malpractice claims and recommends notifying insurers of professional issues.
qs: In Minnesota, 27 lawyers received public discipline in 2024 and 101 received private discipline.

The leading Rule violations cited in Admonitions were: Communications (58); Safekeeping Property (41); Diligence (22); Fees (21); Competence (13); Declining or Terminating Representation (13); and Prejudicial Misconduct (13).
As a reminder, ethical complaints can be the ember for a malpractice claim.

kp.k: Supervision, scope definition, and documentation reduce exposure
kp.d: Bovitz recommends supervisory procedures and training for associates, staff, and lateral hires with supervisory responsibilities. She also recommends written engagement scopes and endpoints, renewed scope acknowledgments for new matters involving existing clients, closing completed matters, oversight of fiduciary roles, calendar and docketing systems, and contemporaneous documentation of critical advice. These are general risk-management recommendations, not AI-specific controls tested by the cited studies.
qs: Implement supervisory procedures and training for associates and staff.
Lateral hires who will serve as “supervisory” lawyers within the structure of your firm should be trained on these procedures and expectations of subordinate and staff supervision.
Engagement agreements should identify the scope of representation and identify when representation will end.
A contemporaneous memo documenting the conversation will serve lawyers and clients well.

kp.k: Client screening must continue throughout representation
kp.d: Bovitz recommends robust conflict checks, qualitative intake, and general-counsel or second-partner approval for clients presenting red flags, including repeated lawyer dismissals, prior claims against counsel, resistance to contacting previous counsel, dubious referrals, and fee litigation. Due diligence should continue as entity leadership or finances change. She urges firms to permit rejection of work regardless of book size, consider withdrawal when clients refuse disclosure, and avoid repeating unverified information in negotiations.
qs: Implement robust conflict procedures, qualitative intake procedures and general counsel or second partner approval are best practices for clients with red flags.
Lawyers should also remember that although a client is a current client, due diligence remains an ongoing consideration.
Firms should send a clear message that lawyers should not be afraid to turn down work from any client no matter the size of the book.
If a client refuses to disclose facts, consider whether withdrawal is necessary.
Do not misstate your client’s financial position and do not simply recite unverified information.

pts.k: Bovitz reports that AI risk is among insurers’ top concerns for major law firms.
pts.d: The source’s only AI-specific claim is a report of insurer concerns identified in the EPIC Study: AI risk appears alongside attorney supervision and cyber risk. Bovitz does not identify particular AI-related failures, quantify AI-related malpractice claims, or predict changes in legal staffing, service delivery or pricing.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is a reported survey of 11 professional liability insurers covering a substantial share of major law firms.
pts.d: Bovitz attributes the finding to Eileen Garczynski’s EPIC Law Firm Group study. The surveyed insurers collectively cover more than 80% of AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 firms. The article supplies no AI-specific claim counts, loss amounts, examples or breakdown of insurer responses; the evidence concerns perceived risk rather than measured AI-caused losses.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The concern is presented as current in 2025, without a forecast horizon.
pts.d: The article was published on 21 October 2025 and cites the EPIC survey announcement dated May 21, 2025. It does not specify the survey’s collection period or conditions under which AI risk materializes. The ABA Study’s separate 2020–2023 data period should not be assigned to the EPIC AI-risk finding.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified exposure concerns AM Law 100 and NLJ 250 insured firms and their professional liability insurers.
pts.d: The claim places AI within the professional liability risk concerns surrounding major law firms. It does not specify effects on particular lawyers, practice areas, clients or the public, and does not extend the AI finding to smaller firms.
